title: GLP-1 Weight Loss Drugs Linked to Higher Risk of Hair Loss, Studies Find
excerpt: University of Pennsylvania researchers found users of drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro faced up to 68% higher odds of alopecia, though absolute rates remain low at 3 to 9 per 1,000 patients per year.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 drug users face 37% to 68% higher alopecia risk than other diabetes medication users.
  • Alopecia rates are low, at 3 to 9 per 1,000 patients annually, primarily non-scarring.
  • Tirzepatide users experience higher alopecia rates (4.24%) than semaglutide users (3.33%).
  • Rapid weight loss and nutrient deficiencies may contribute to increased hair loss risk.
  • Hair loss from GLP-1 drugs is typically reversible, impacting treatment decisions.

People taking popular GLP-1 weight loss drugs face a measurably higher risk of hair loss than those on other diabetes medications, according to multiple studies published this week that provide the most systematic evidence yet of the side effect.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine analyzed electronic health records from over 50,000 adults with type 2 diabetes treated at Penn Medicine between January 2019 and September 2024. Their findings, published Wednesday in The BMJ, showed that GLP-1 users had 37% higher odds of developing alopecia compared to users of SGLT-2 inhibitors and 68% higher odds compared to those on DPP-4 inhibitors, after adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, body mass index, and pre-existing conditions.

Low Absolute Risk, but Real Consequences

The study compared 12,004 GLP-1 users against 15,221 SGLT-2 users and 11,964 GLP-1 users against 11,233 DPP-4 users over an average follow-up of 2.7 years. Actual alopecia rates ranged from about 3 to 9 per 1,000 people per year — low in absolute terms, but enough to affect treatment decisions for some patients.

"Although hair loss does not typically result in physical harm, it may have significant psychosocial consequences, affecting self-esteem, quality of life, and adherence to treatment."

— Dr. Yong Chen, University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine

The association was specific to non-scarring alopecia — a form where hair follicles remain intact, leaving the door open for regrowth. Compared to the two control drug classes, non-scarring alopecia risk was 53% and 72% higher in GLP-1 users, respectively.

Tirzepatide Carries Higher Risk Than Semaglutide

A third study, conducted by Cambridge, Massachusetts-based analytics firm nference and submitted as a preprint, compared 11,046 patients on tirzepatide — sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound by Eli Lilly — with the same number on semaglutide, marketed by Novo Nordisk as Ozempic and Wegovy. New-onset alopecia rates were 4.24% with tirzepatide and 3.33% with semaglutide. Among women, the gap was wider: 5.44% versus 3.63%.

The nference researchers found that the elevated risk persisted regardless of how much weight patients lost or how much of the drug they received, suggesting factors beyond simple weight loss may be at work.

"This supports more individualized counseling and surveillance rather than a generic message that weight loss itself inevitably causes hair loss."

— Venky Soundararajan, nference

A separate study published in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology, drawing on data from more than 1 million participants worldwide, found significantly higher risks of various alopecia subtypes with GLP-1 drugs compared to metformin, a widely prescribed diabetes medication.

Mechanism: Weight Loss, Nutrient Gaps, or Something Else?

The Penn researchers pointed to rapid weight loss and reduced caloric intake as the most likely explanations. Caloric restriction can trigger physiological stress and deficiencies in iron, zinc, and biotin — all critical to the hair growth cycle. Hormonal and immunological effects of GLP-1 drugs on hair follicles may also contribute, though more research is needed.

In the UK, more than 1,250 patients have reported hair loss as a side effect of Wegovy, Mounjaro, or Ozempic since early 2025, according to health officials. Britain's National Institute of Health and Care Excellence already classifies hair loss as a "common or very common" side effect of GLP-1 drugs.

What This Means for Patients

All three research teams emphasized that hair loss associated with GLP-1 drugs is typically reversible. Chen wrote that awareness of the risk should inform shared decision-making between patients and their doctors, even if the absolute numbers are small. For the millions of people globally using these medications — including a growing number in the Indian diaspora managing weight or diabetes — the findings add a new dimension to weigh alongside the drugs' well-documented benefits for cardiovascular health and weight management.

The Penn researchers acknowledged limitations, including a lack of data on severity, duration, and whether alopecia reversed after patients stopped treatment. They noted that unmeasured factors could have influenced results, but called their data high-quality and their findings consistent across multiple analyses.
